title: Act for Health 2.0: How We Can “ACT for Health” - ACT for Health 2.0 Comparison of an “ACT for Health” intervention (self-study)—a prevention program based on Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) designed to promote students’ mental health—with a waiting-list control group
summary: Students’ mental health deteriorates over the course of their studies. This randomized controlled pilot study examines whether a newly developed self-study workbook based on Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) can be effectively implemented by undergraduate psychology students and whether it shows initial evidence of effects comparable to those of ACT training led by peer health coaches. Participants will be randomly assigned (1:1:1) to the training group, the self-study group, or a waiting-list control group. The primary outcome measure is the change in psychological flexibility; in addition, psychological distress, emotion regulation, well-being, resilience, self-compassion, as well as feasibility and acceptance will be assessed.

interventions.name: Established ACT prevention program “ACT for Health” in a group setting (approx. 10 students), led by two trained peer health coaches (master’s students in psychology/psychotherapy) under the supervision of experienced psychotherapists: Introductory session (120 min.), 8 weekly training sessions (90

The same ten modules, completed independently using the newly developed “ACT for Health” workbook; weekly delivery of learning materials at the same frequency as during the training; in-person introductory and concluding sessions.
No intervention during the study period; participation in all surveys; access to the workbook after data collection is complete.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Bachelor's students in the Psychology program at the University of Lübeck; age 18 or older; German-speaking; written consent following verbal and written informed consent
Exclusion criteria:
Individuals who are foreseeably unable to participate regularly and fully in the program being offered; those currently experiencing an acute mental illness or undergoing ongoing psychotherapy
